newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agency proposes new rules for car airbags.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agency proposes new rules for car airbags.

text.p: Federal regulators on Friday proposed new rules for car airbags to allow them to inflate with less explosive force and reduce the risk of injury to children and to small and frail adults.

In addition to cutting their explosive force -- the bags inflate at up to 200 miles an hour (322 kph) -- the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration proposed letting owners disconnect their passenger-side airbag.

While airbags were credited with saving more than 1,500 lives in the past 10 years, they were also blamed for the deaths of at least 30 children, many of whom were riding in front seats or were unbuckled when the bags deployed.
"Airbags are working well but need to be improved to enhance the safety of children and small-stature adults," NHTSA Administrator Ricardo Martinez said in a statement.
Officials said a slower inflation rate would continue to protect adults in most high speed crashes, yet lower the risk to children and small adults.
The NHTSA has been under increasing pressure to make airbags safer.
Public Citizen, a Ralph Nader-founded advocacy group, urged the agency to require dual-inflation bags that would inflate rapidly in high speed crashes but slower in less severe crashes.
But the NHTSA said it would take at least three years for those to be developed and installed and action was needed now.

The NHTSA said its proposals were steps toward the installation of a so-called smart airbag that would sense when a child or small adult was in the passenger seat and lower the bag's inflation force accordingly.
Martinez told a news conference that the agency's aim was to begin to phase-in the "smart" bags in the autumn of 1998 for the 1999 car model year.
Before the smart bags are developed, the inflation force of the bags would be cut by 20-35 percent on new cars within a year.

Asked if lowering the inflation force increased risk for adults, Martinez said tests showed the concept "allows us to decrease most of those risks and still retain the benefits for unbelted occupants."
Martinez said starting in 90 days cars would be required to have a warning label telling parents airbags could be dangerous to children and that children should always ride buckled in the rear seat.
The NHTSA's proposal to allow car owers to deactivate passenger-side bags eases current regulations that sharply restrict deactivation.
Previously deactivation was only allowed for reasons that included medical concerns, short stature and for people who have reasonable concerns about airbag safety.

Under the new regulation mechanics will be asked to provide customers wanting to deactivate their airbag with NHTSA information on airbags and owners will be required to post a warning in their car to tell riders the car's airbag has been disabled.
